When I created ICBM Attack, I wanted to do a 'trackball' controller, like what Missile Command had. But that would have been a more complex design.

A trackball controller is a "chopper wheel" mechanism which provides pulses which can be counted to determine speed and direction (using both X and Y inputs).
An inverted trackball was in fact the first form of a 'computer mouse'.
A trackball is a differential based system, where the input signal is relative, not absolute.

Unfortunately the Bally Arcade uses an absolute tracking system. The 50k potentiomater that is used by the knob for determining 'how much' rotation there is.
Creating a controller using two knobs (one for X, and the other for Y) yields an analog XY Joystick. (Which is what the ICBM Attack controller is,)

Starting with a trackball as the controller, would not only mean converting the electrical interface, but converting the input signal itself.
Method 1 would be to create a circuit that tracked the trackball and converted the differential signals from the trackball into an absolute signal (a 0 to 50k resistance). The advantage of this system is that it would work with the existing cartridge and software. The downside is that it is a fairly complex design, and would take a fair amount of design time to build. Sadly, time that I do not have.
Method 2 would be to change the software to accept differential signals. This 'could be' done, but again, it would require a fair amount of software modification. Code would have to be written to support the trackball. And that would take a fair amount of time for this method as well. On the plus side, supporting a trackball would also basically mean you would have a routine to support a mouse input. And yes, it is technically possible that mouse support could be added to the Bally Arcade via a new input routine. But again, the amount of work to do this is extensive.
Method 3 would use the emulator to interface to a trackball and provide a 0-255 value to the code (what the A/D input produces from the 50k potentiometer). This seems like the most reasonable path to me. Taking an existing trackball controller that can be supported in an emulator like MAME, and having an interface routine that converts the differential signals from the trackball into an absolute 0-255 signal that is provided to the game. This means that the ICBM Attack code would not have to be modified and would be the path of 'least resistance' as far as time and resources are concerned.

Well, that's my two cents worth...
Brett

👾 Z80 assembly source code, binaries, and dev tools for the Bally Astrocade game console. - hxlnt/astrocade
github.com
One of Rachel's programs is Astroimg, a Python command-line tool that converts images to Z80 assembly.

I've attached an example of a converted picture.

Rachel also has Astropaint there, a browser-based tool that she used for drawing original Astrocade background graphics.

I highly recommend anyone interested in Asrtocade programming to check out her GitHub page.

2)  zhuowei / Nyastrocat - A demo for the Bally Astrocade. Currently plays the Nyan Cat song in a loop. This one hasn't been updated since August 2013.

https://github.com/zhuowei/Nyastrocat

3) MAMEdev - astrohome.cpp - This is the Astrocade driver.  I'm not sure if this is the official site.

https://github.com/mamedev/mame/commits/0f0d39ef81562c75e79176dd3bebb1e491ca39d5/src/mame/drivers/astrohome.cpp

4)  iscarabaid / astrocade - Nathan Altice's Bally Astrocade code repository. Created March 2018.

https://github.com/iscarabaid/astrocade

5)  rzurad / wizard-of-wor - Web browser port of the 1981 Midway Games title "Wizard of Wor" for Bally Astrocade.  Last updated May 2017.  Does anyone want to try this one out?

https://github.com/rzurad/wizard-of-wor

6)  MiSTer-devel / Astrocade_MiSTer - This is an FPGA implementation of the Bally Astrocade based on a project by MikeJ.  I think that this one stays pretty current.  Someone just commented on my ICBM Attack video that they use MiSTer for Astrocade FPGA "emulation" and that they'd like to add trackball support for their FPGA system to play ICBM Attack.

https://github.com/MiSTer-devel/Astrocade_MiSTer

Bally Astrocade for MiSTer This is an FPGA implementation of the Bally Astrocade based on a project by MikeJ. Features. Supports full keypad. Supports paddle control as analog stick.
github.com

https://github.com/zhuowei/jsbally-proto

https://github.com/sehugg/happy2020

When I created ICBM Attack, I wanted to do a 'trackball' controller, like what Missile Command had. But that would have been a more complex design.

A trackball controller is a "chopper wheel" mechanism which provides pulses which can be counted to determine speed and direction (using both X and Y inputs).
An inverted trackball was in fact the first form of a 'computer mouse'.
A trackball is a differential based system, where the input signal is relative, not absolute.

Unfortunately the Bally Arcade uses an absolute tracking system. The 50k potentiomater that is used by the knob for determining 'how much' rotation there is.
Creating a controller using two knobs (one for X, and the other for Y) yields an analog XY Joystick. (Which is what the ICBM Attack controller is,)

Starting with a trackball as the controller, would not only mean converting the electrical interface, but converting the input signal itself.
Method 1 would be to create a circuit that tracked the trackball and converted the differential signals from the trackball into an absolute signal (a 0 to 50k resistance). The advantage of this system is that it would work with the existing cartridge and software. The downside is that it is a fairly complex design, and would take a fair amount of design time to build. Sadly, time that I do not have.
Method 2 would be to change the software to accept differential signals. This 'could be' done, but again, it would require a fair amount of software modification. Code would have to be written to support the trackball. And that would take a fair amount of time for this method as well. On the plus side, supporting a trackball would also basically mean you would have a routine to support a mouse input. And yes, it is technically possible that mouse support could be added to the Bally Arcade via a new input routine. But again, the amount of work to do this is extensive.
Method 3 would use the emulator to interface to a trackball and provide a 0-255 value to the code (what the A/D input produces from the 50k potentiometer). This seems like the most reasonable path to me. Taking an existing trackball controller that can be supported in an emulator like MAME, and having an interface routine that converts the differential signals from the trackball into an absolute 0-255 signal that is provided to the game. This means that the ICBM Attack code would not have to be modified and would be the path of 'least resistance' as far as time and resources are concerned.

Well, that's my two cents worth...
Brett

16759:
In about 1984 I picked up a CX-22 trackball (a brown one with yellow buttons) at KB Toys, new in the box, for $5.  This was during the time when so many Atari games were being blown out the door for practically free.  There was a huge selection of games to choose from for the Atari 2600 and some other game systems.  One table was just full of trackballs.  I was about twelve years old at the time and I picked up the trackball to use it with my Commodore 64.  I used the trackball in joystick mode to play Atarisoft's C64 versions of Centipede and Crystal Castles.  The trackball worked wonderfully and mimicked a true trackball even in joystick mode for these two games.  Man, how I loved to spin that trackball like crazy to make my way about the maze with Bentley Bear!

Later on, in the early-to-mid 1990s, I would use an Atari trackball to play Missile Command on my Atari 800XL in true trackball mode.  This mode was built into the Missile Command cartridge and could be accessed by pressing Control-T.

Dan Kramer, who designed the Atari 2600 and 5200 trackball, made his own three-button trackball controller (see attached picture) for a modified version of Missile Command for the Atari 8-bit that could fire from three different bases.  You can see that controller here:

https://atariage.com/forums/gallery/image/20236-dan-kramer-3-fire-button-custom-trak-ball-controller/

There's more information in this thread:

http://www.dragonslairfans.com/smfor/index.php?topic=5967.0

Here's a video of Dan showing off his CX-22 trackball (which he also designed):

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nNZpwGWLDZk
[https://i.ytimg.com/vi/nNZpwGWLDZk/maxresdefault.jpg]<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nNZpwGWLDZk>
Dan Kramer Trackball - YouTube<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nNZpwGWLDZk>
Dan "the man" Kramer TB. Dan designed the trackballs for Atari, and made some cool modifications to play Missile Command and the Atari 5200 Tempest. Neat!
www.youtube.com
I have two beat-up, partially working CX-22 trackballs in the garage someplace.  Maybe I'll drag them out and see if I can get some help to make one function properly.

Adam

16768:
I let a hi-res update slip by me a couple of weeks ago.  Here are two updates in one post (one is from today).

Michael updated me again about his hi-res project(s) on January 13, 2020.  Here are Michael's comments:

----------------------------------------

Subject: Multi-Pager Test Demo Update

All 8 pages have been programmed with static graphics. A variable speed page flipper routine, including a flip sound, is finished and working. At maximum speed,  pages are flipped about every 1/4 second. I'm beginning to work on the moving critter who is getting very hungry to eat up most of the 8 pages of static graphics. It looks like the demo is going to be under 6KB leaving nearly 2.5KB for the upgraded hi-res Fish Demo. I have big graphic plans for this hi-res Fish Demo. I can already see it running in my mind. I'm hoping I can realize that vision with 2KB of EEPROM.

The static graphics in pages 6 and 7 get a real workout by the Z80 CPU. For example, when the demo text intro in page 0 is initially being viewed, not only is the Z80 utilizing multiple magic functions to write graphics into pages 6 and 7, but it is also working the stack area executing call/return and push/pop instructions in these 2 pages plus it is working with some variables in the scratchpad area. This is a significant test demonstrating that the Z80 can write to or read a user selected page while viewing another page on the TV screen.

The multi-pager hardware is working great. No surprise there, since the multi-pager hardware on my modified for hi-res static screen RAM Astrocade is a near copy of the Data Max UV-1R multi-pager hardware.

I am now being visually rewarded for all my hard work designing, building and testing this one-of-a-kind hi-res Astrocade. I am very pleased with its performance.

This new demo is looking really good to me. Wait till you see the hi-res Gunfight screenshot on page 7. In case you're wondering, MCM Design has no plans to convert the low-res Gunfight into hi-res. I chose a hi-res Gunfight screenshot for page 7 because it really shows off the hi-res screen resolution capability of the custom address and data chips in a "modified for hi-res" Astrocade.

Bye.
MCM

----------------------------------------

Lance Squire commented, "This sounds amazing.  I would love to see video of it when done."

This does sound fantastic to me too.  It's always a thrill to get an update from Michael... which is why I'm making this post, as he sent me his newest update this morning (February 4, 2020).  Here's what Michael says:

----------------------------------------

Subject: Multi-Pager Test Demo Update

I'm pleased to announce MCM Design has completed its multi-pager test demo/demonstration. It is an awesome demo. The demo description emailed to you previously has been 100% realized. The demo utilizes 5716 bytes leaving 2476 bytes for the hi-res upgraded Fish Demo, which will be attached to the end of the multi-pager demo.

Multipage programming is a new experience. Debugging the Move Critter routine was a challenge. This routine was another major test for the multi-pager. The Move Critter's main program is executed in the page 7 scratchpad area. The Z80 stack area is also switched to pages 0 thru 6 for the critter write routine. So, the challenge arose because the Z80 stack was switching back and forth from page 7 to the other pages, plus there was a screen interrupt countdown timer to deal with. You have to really pay attention to what is going on, always looking at the programming from the Z80's perspective. The screen interrupt issue was eventually resolved simply by adding a DI, EI instruction before and after the critter write subroutine, so this write routine couldn't be interrupted.

The vertical blank register is dropped all the way down during the Move Critter execution. You can easily see the Z80 working the stack PUSH/POP instructions during the critter write routine execution in pages 0 thru 6. You can also see the main Move Critter program of 98 bytes loaded into the bottom 2 lines in the page 7 screen RAM. This visual confirmation of what the demo is doing in the multi-pager during the Move Critter execution is a cool visual experience. The 98 byte main program was copied from cartridge ROM to page 7 screen RAM beginning at 7F20H. A jump to 7F20H followed the copy routine so that the Z80 would start executing the main program at 7F20H in page 7.

I decided to add one more short test demo. This demo will execute when a certain column key is held down while pressing the system reset button. There will be 3 connecting scenes (pages) with simplified static graphics to visually determine which scene is being viewed. A critter will initially appear in the center scene. The critter will be movable only using a hand control (input port #1).

This new demo will test how the multi-pager will react to the critter moving from the center to left scenes and back, plus the center to right scenes and back. This demo shouldn't take too many bytes. I am expecting at least 2K bytes available for the hi-res Fish Demo. I'm looking forward to seeing this hi-res Fish Demo executing. Hi-res rocks!

I also look forward to mailing you [Adam] my DVD so others can experience the New World of a hi-res multi-paging Astrocade. Too bad the Astrocade community doesn't have access to this kind of an Astrocade.

Bye.
MCM

----------------------------------------

Michael is really committed to sharing his worth with all of us.  I love it!

You can read the hi-res thread on AtariAge, which includes this post and many others which are related to it, here:

https://atariage.com/forums/topic/254592-hi-res-bally-arcadeastrocade-correspondence/?do=findComment&comment=4449483

Every time I read Michael's updates I want to see his work in person.

16770:
The Bally Arcade/Astrocade emulation in MAME 0.207 was the last version that supported four controllers.  I noticed this when I was trying to setup ICBM Attack's Spectre controller to work with the Astrocade.  I had to use an older version of MAME to get the controller to work.

Beginning in MAME version 0.208, the first version where "Just Desserts" added 2000-baud tape support for Bally BASIC (AstroBASIC), MAME only supports one controller port.   I'm not sure if the Astrocade's other controller ports were removed on purpose, or if this was done by accident? I'm really surprised that no one noticed this change to MAME.  There are many two-player games for the Astrocade; I guess that the Astrocade emulation gets used less than I thought with the gaming community.

Tape support for the Astrocade was added in March 2019 in a thread called "Bounty: $100 for Astrocade Tape Support," here:

https://forums.bannister.org/ubbthreads.php?ubb=showflat&Number=114841&#Post114841

I just sent "Just Desserts" a personal message in the Bannister forums asking if there is a way to add support for all four controllers again without losing tape support.  Hopefully I hear back from him soon.

Adam

16772:
"Just Desserts" replied to me.  He said:

"It's not "lost", it just doesn't default to having four controllers plugged in.  Run MAME with -listslots to list what optional slots the Astrocade has, and what you can plug into them."

I did this and I got a long listing.  From inside MAME I turned on the slot device for "ctrl2" and the joystick port worked okay. The default configuration for the joystick conflicts with the keypad, but I changed that easily enough from within MAME.

Also, even though I know "Just Desserts" was not able to get the 300-baud cassette tape interface working, the, I guess, preliminary support is shown in the slot devices.  Each "ctrl" port 1-4 allows the MAME user to choose "cassette," even though the 300-baud tape interface only works when plugged into port 3 (and the light pen port).

I've attached a text file I put together with the slot devices all listed.  I've also pasted it below my signature, but the formatting will all be lost.

Adam

Astrocade MAME Slots
--------------------
February 11, 2020
Compiled by Adam Trionfo

This list of slots available for the Bally Arcade/Astrocade was created using
the 64-bit version of MAME 0.209 with the the command line:

mame64 astrocde -listslots

Thanks to "Just Desserts" on the MAME forums at:

https://forums.bannister.org/

He helped me figure-out why only one slot comes up by default.

                                  blue_ram_32k     Bally Astrocade Blue RAM 32K
                                  blue_ram_4k      Bally Astrocade Blue RAM 4K
                                  lil_white_ram    Bally Astrocade Lil' White RAM 32K
                                  rl64_ram         Bally Astrocade R&L RAM 64K
                                  viper_sys1       Bally Astrocade Viper System 1

                 cartslot         [none]           No options available

The ONLY area you cannot use is the VIDEO ram. For the standard HVGS system thatn is from 4000 hex to 4FFF hex. The cartridge area (2000 hex to 3FFF hex) can be used by the 128K cart. The OBR (OM) can be altered using code inside the 128K. so, theoretically speaking, 60K is feasible, but not typically practical.Naturally the Hi-Res needs more Video RAM, so that's where the 48K limit would exist.

16787:
Given the amount of work that it would take to actually make a high res arcade work right, I believe it would be easier to simply emulate the arcade on a FPGA.

This has been done for some arcade games...
https://github.com/nullobject/rygar-fpga
https://www.fpgaarcade.com

And it seems that some folks have looked into downloading MAME into FPGAs...
https://www.jackenhack.com/mister-fpga-getting-arcade-cores-to-use-mra-files/

Anyway, regardless of any other efforts, designing an FPGA based on MAME code and modifying the code to support the higher resolution, I feel would be a simpler and more usable solution. That said, games for this High Res Bally emulation would have to written to use the higher resolution.

So, why have I never done this?

I pondered creating a 'high res' version of an arcade for about a 1/10 of a second, before realizing that the result would not be a "Bally Arcade". In that it would not run older cartridges in high resolution (they games would have to be rewritten to use the higher resolution). And that just scaling up the old cartridges would look the same as just playing the old games as they are.

We did a trick like this when we created the first iPad. The iPad was simply 4 times the resolution of the iPhone. So any iPhone App could run with doubled X and Y resolutions to 'fill' the iPad screen. The point was to emulate existing apps on new hardware (i.e. a bigger screen). With the expectation that native apps would be written for the iPad later (and they were...).

But creating a high res Bally machine and emulating the old cartridges does not have any specific advantages, especially for the amount of work it takes...

If you want an easer way to create a higher resolution Bally Arcade, perhaps take an old Bally Arcade Commercial game (GORF, Wizard of War, etc.) and start there. A game like that would already be operating the custom chips in High Res commercial mode. All you would have to do is build an interface from the 'game board'. I remember that those games had a card cage that had a board specific to the game, but the rest of the system was pretty generic.

In fact, saying that now, if I were trying to create a high res Bally arcade, I would take one of the old commercial arcade games, and just design a cartridge emulator board. Something that you could download code to and just plug that into the card cage. The I/O board might need to be modified to support more controls if you wished, but that would not be that hard.

Unfortunately, it is still a lot of effort. And not something I have interest in doing.

But that's my 2 cents,
Brett

customs to put up 320 pixels per line at 2 bits per pixel color. There is a Tony Miller explanation here: https://ballyalley.com/faqs/bally_professional_arcade_video_hardware_faq.zip at Bally Alley. He goes into detail

There is some hi-res Z80 assembly code available on BallyAlley.com already.  Some requires a modified Astrocade and some attempts to run on a stock unit.

1) BalCheckHR.
Z80 Assembly Language Source Code.
By MCM Design (Michael Matte).
2019.

This is about 180 pages of handwritten, Z80 assembly language software for the BalCheckHR unit. This hardware allows experienced electronics users to diagnose many problems with a Bally Arcade/Astrocade game console. This device has many improvements over the original BalCheckHR hardware, including special routines to test Astrocade units that have been modified to use high-res mode. This BalCheck software, if you were to type it in, would assemble to an 8K ROM image. On the BalCheckHR hardware, this is bank 0 of the 32K ROM.

https://ballyalley.com/ml/ml_source/ml_source.html#BalCheckHRZ80SourceCode


2) Hi-Res Textured 10 Color Test Pattern
By Michael Matte / MCM Design
Written in 2017.

This program is an upgraded hi-res version of Bit Fiddler's "Standard Color Generator" listed in the Machine Language Manager's User Manual on page 7-4. This output a very cool graphic pattern on a 20" RF TV using composite video output. The routine is self-supporting and uses NO outside CALLs.

Michael says, "Have fun mixing up colors and hi-res texture. You can change the surrounding border. You can also change the vertical bar color/textures in the pixel set. You can display solid colors or textures colors. Note that even though 8 colors were specified, the texturing effect in routine yields 2 additional colors. So, the routine displays ten colors total.

"Wish you could see this hi-res test pattern on my 20" Toshiba using my hi-res Astrocade with composite video signal output. it is so cool. Here's hoping you can share this experience on the MAME emulator."

https://ballyalley.com/ml/ml_homebrew/ml_homebrew.html#MLHiResTextured10ColorTestPattern


3) Hi-Res Demo Program.
By Adam Trionfo.
2002.

This program displays, in hi-res, 16 pixels starting at $4000 (the top-left side of the screen). The colors are repeated twice (two whites together, two blacks together, etc) so that they can be disguised from each other. This program works on the Astrocade emulator in MAME, but not a real Astrocade (although it will probably work on an Astrocade modified for hi-res mode). This program only displays in the top-left 1/4 of the screen (since the Astrocade only has 4K of RAM and this isn't really "true" hi-res [there's not 16K]).

The programs in this archive are:

    hi-res (Screenshot).gif - A screenshot of this program running.
    hi-res.bin - This is the binary. If it is run in Astrocade emulator in MAME, then the program will run. This binary should probably also work on an Astrocade that has been modified for hi-res mode.
    hi-res.lst
    hi-res.z80 - The Z80 source code for this program. This can be assembled use the Zmac assembler.
    HVGLIB.H - Home Video Game Library equates file. This program is required to assemble the hi-res source code.

https://ballyalley.com/ml/ml_homebrew/ml_homebrew.html#Hi-ResHomebrew

So, there's not a lot of hi-res code... but there is a bit of it written already.  MAME doesn't support hi-res mode, at least not in the same way as Michael Matte's high-res unit works, which mimics the UV-1 hardware.

16812:
Steve you asked for some suggestions and ideas about your astrocade dream project.  Here are my thoughts and ideas.

I think that you probably have peaked the interest of many people in this discussion group.  Your proposal seems very time-consuming.  I don't doubt your enthusiasm but do you have the time to work on a project of this magnitude?  Would you be working on it alone?

Here are my specific comments on your proposed ideas so far:

1) Using a real "Z80" (or, rather the ez80 which I think is considered to be 100% compatible and available directly from Zilog) is certainly the way to go with this project.  One of the stumbling blocks that other projects of this kind encounter is that softcore CPUs tend not to be 100% cycle accurate.  Using a real soup would fix this issue.  I have not looked recently, but isn't the ez80 discontinued?  Is there an easy source to find them now?

2) I can understand why you don't want to include the code for the 8K onboard ROM.  Are you proposing that someone desolder the ROM from their astrocade motherboard?  Would you have some sort of EEPROM socket included on the board?  Even better would be a way to load the ROM from some sort of memory card.  This feature would allow one to easily skip the onboard ROM for Hi-Res applications, for I believe once the astrocade is put into low-Res mode via the on-board ROM, there is no easy way to go "backward" to Hi-Res mode.  Or is there?

3) The 8K of cart space is of course required to be compatible with an astrocade.  Using a bank switching scheme here would be appropriate.  Especially if it uses the scheme that Steve Tucker
created for his 512K bank switched cart (essentially one 4K fixed bank with many other banks which can be switched in and out of "ROM").

4) Up to 48K of RAM would be awesome.  The 64K RAM Board by R&L Enterprises offers a slew of different ways to change which RAM/ROM is accessed.  Perhaps the manual for that expansion port might provide some ideas it's for you.  It is available here:

https://ballyalley.com/documentation/misc_hardware_docs/full_size/64k_ram_board.pdf

5) Low-res mode is the most essential mode of operation for any Astrocade compatible system.  Hi-Res mode would give it a similar capability to that of the arcade units.  As for medium-res mode, can you explain some advantages that it would offer to users/programmers?  Does it come "free" with hi-res or would it require additional "hardware?"

6) Compatibility with all the original Astrocade connectors would certainly be an added bonus, but with the seemingly off-putting problem of making the unit difficult to create and manufacture at an affordable price.

As for some of the possible features that you list:

7) Keyboard compatibility with a standard USB keyboard seems fantastic.  It would be interesting to see how different modes of operation for the shift keys would work.  For instance, there would still need to be some method to access the WORDS key for BASIC.

8 and 9) A disk or hard drive would not be required for the system.  If SDRAM were available then I imagine that would be the best method to use to save/load.  Perhaps the SD RAM could be used for tape images?

Your goal of getting the astrocade working as it is out-of-the-box from 1978 is an essential first step, as you mentioned.  As you said, this project would need to crawl before it could walk or even "run."

Even if this project never materializes in any manner whatsoever, it's fun to talk about this stuff in a discussion group.  You have the right setting here to bounce ideas off of people who understand what you're talking about with this, as of now, just shooting-the-breeze discussion.  If something becomes of this project then I'm all for it.  If this project just stays in let's-talk-about-it mode, that I'm all for that too.

Adam

16826:
I'd be interested in buying at least two of those, depending on the cost.

I think the best known drop ins for vintage systems are the Ultimate 64

https://ultimate64.com/Ultimate-64

and the C64 Reloaded

https://icomp.de/shop-icomp/en/produkt-details/product/c64-reloaded-mk2.html

I think it's worth taking a look at their approaches because they cover
much of what most retro-enthusiasts need. You can see they take different
approaches to the ICs- one is an FPGA implementation, and the other uses
real chips. Both fit perfectly in an original C64 case without
modification, which is crucial. I think for storage, it's best just to use
a flash card solution and skip the spinning drives.

I understand it's a feasibility study. The problem is, the Astrocade is
uncommon. You could probably find 25 or 40 people to sacrifice an Astrocade
for a modern upgrade in the first year, I think over the years you could
sell a few more dozen, maybe even 100. The problem is, as a product, the
break even is probably at 50 or 75 units sold (considering the cost of
ordering a bunch of units). And that is if you don't have to undergo
multiple revisions based on function or port positioning, which are costly.

I'm sure it's just an engineering exercise for you, but if you did make a
production run, I be massively appreciative. Or you could find a company
that does retro-hardware interested in dealing with the production if you
want to do the design.

You might also consider taking a look at the arcade boards that were
considered to be similar to an "Astrocade II" design.

-ian

David, you makes some good points about this project not being a real Astrocade.  I agree with you on every point.  That being said, the Astrocade will always be there to be used in its 1978 configuration.  Everything that is being talked about here has been done for other platforms.  The C64 had "upgrades" like the C128 and the Commodore 65 (an unreleased, rather crazy system).  The Atari 400 had it's big brother the 800, then the 1200XL, the 800XL, the XE line and now the modern systems.  I can think of many other examples.  Tech-people want to push their personal favorite computer and game systems.  Imagine if the original IBM PC from 1981 had stayed stagnant.  The only way to run that software now is via emulation on a modern PC... yet modern PCs all can trace their roots back to that clunky, expensive system.

Personally, I'd like a simple Astrocade upgrade that just gave me a motherboard like Sea Wolf II, but any new hardware being worked on for the Astrocade-- or even just discussed that turns out to never take any steps toward completion (not that I'm saying this about this project)-- is fine by me.

Back in the early 2000s I said something in these forums along the lines of "A system is only dead when people stop making new hardware and software for it."  Therefore, based on even just the talk of this project it can be easily concluded that the Astrocade isn't dead.  Hooray!

I've not had any trouble getting MAME to work with homemade software for the Astrocade.  Try running anything you write from the command line.  My preferred command line for MAME is:

mame64 astrocde -cart astrobas -nofilter -keepaspect -window

This command line will load and run AstroBASIC.  If you replace the name of the cartridge with the path and title of your program, then any cartridge should run okay.

Here is another example:

mame64 astrocde -cart H:\Astrocade_02\_Programming_(Test_Area)\MAME\mame0200b_64bit\Homebrew\astrocade_xm_test.bin -debug -nofilter

This runs a homebrew program (that's not available to the public) using MAME's debugger.

The overscan area was required for older TVs.  Not all TVs show the overscan area.  This isn't really an issue anymore with modern TVs-- even including CRTs from the (about) mid-1980s and onward, but this was a major concern for older TVs.  I have two CRTs and both show more or less of the overscan area using the same Astrocade.  Some old TVs would even encroach on how much of the non-overscan that was shown.  While there is a long tradition of using the overscan area of many home computers, it's probably best not to use tricks like this one.

Adam

16863:
Yes... Where modern Digital TV formats display all the pixels and did not require 'scanning' the display, the older Analog TV format had horizontal and vertical blanking signals, and a line scanning system.

The only way on old analog TVs not to see this 'blanking' area was to overscan the display (meaning part of the TV picture was lost being 'scanned' off the edges of the display).

That was 'ok' for TV pictures, all that happened was you lost a little bit of the picture. But, when digital signals (converted to analog for display) came along, if you used the entire picture display area for a game, then part of the display was not shown. And usually that would be things like the score at the top of the screen, or the goal nets in a game of soccer. So, having an 'overscan' area that could be sacrificed to the old analog TV's displays was the only reliable way for video games to be fully displayed on the screen.

The 'overscan' area does not use memory. It is simply a blanking signal. In fact, in the arcade, there are registers for setting and adjusting the 'blanking overscan'. I changed the settings in one of my games so that I could 'steal' some of the screen memory to use as scratch RAM for the game. 😁

Most kids today have no idea that on old TV sets, we had to manually adjust some of the parameters on a TV set to just get a signal. Including adjusting the frequency of the TV channel, adjusting the vertical and horizontal hold, etc... If you did not, then the picture would 'roll' or be unstable...

https://blurbusters.com/photo-of-analog-vsync-signal/

For those interested, here is some history...
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analog_television

I actually wrote an early article on the "Transition to Digital" and participated with the working group that came up with the ATSC formats.

The Bally arcade opened the door for me to start down a path of learning about both computers, and TV signals. I ended up building a video board (The Video Explorer) with some other engineers, and eventually led the team at Apple that create the Mac Mini and Apple TV products. We even did iPad prototypes...

It was pretty cool going from TV sets that were in B&W to today's 4K Digital TVs.

There is an area of "overscan" called the vertical retrace area. This area is where the TY studios used to do such things as sync the scan oascillators (both Vert and Horiz), syncronize the colors, and various other items. This was evident whin you were able to tae the Vert hold control and turn it so that you could see the "blacker-than-black" bar. In the middle was the "Belt and Buckle" which was all of the studio's scratchpad. in B&W sets it was various shades orf gray. The color sets looked much prettier. This area, verticle retrace, is where good programmers do a lot of overhead like do the math and "show" for the moving of the gtraphics. 16872:
Ken brings up some incredibly good reasons to steer clear of the NTSC signal that the Astrocade uses if the system is to be re-created on an FPGA chip.  He also brings up some wonderful reasons to keep the original Astrocade around: it is one of the earliest technologies that was able to work its way around an standard NTSC signal and keep it within the standards that were required for broadcast signals.

I've got my reservations about a new FPGA astrocade.  I want one to exist.  If it was here in my office right now, then-- hell, yeah!-- I would hook it up and use it right away.  I just happen to see, I think the incredibly time-consuming efforts of Steve.  These might be used on a hardware project that could easily consume years of time.  I say that from a realistic point of view.  From a dream-perspective, I would like to see Steve work on and complete this project with a community of effort working with him.  I'm not sure if that is possible or if he wants to work on this project alone.  Whatever the case, I give him my best wishes for this project.

I have been working on archiving Bally Arcade/Astrocade material for a couple of decades now.  Every once in a while there is the scent of something new in the community and I get excited about it.  This is one of those times.  Other projects that piqued my interest and came into existence are the UltiMulti cartridge, the Lil' White RAM and the two homebrew cartridges that were released.

The first time that the FPGA astrocade came up in conversation and was actually created, this sort of hardware was very expensive.  Since 2002, when the idea first blew its way across the astrocade scene, the hardware has come down in price significantly.  Perhaps it is now that such a project as Steve proposes can come into existence.

Getting back once again to Ken's look into TV signals in the overscan area.  The Atari 2600 has always been one of my favorite game systems.  With that system the programmers had to "chase the beam" (as it has come to be called), following the TV signal as it was drawn to the screen.  Luckily for astrocade programmers, this didn't have to be done.

Only recently has this "chasing the beam" topic come up again.  From what I understand from the programmer who created the "Astrocademo" (Genesis Project), the astrocade could draw in what would look like Hi-Res mode.  However, it would require programming the astrocade in much the same way that the Atari 2600 is programmed.  There seems to be little point in using the astrocade in this manner, for it is counter-intuitive and, perhaps, counter-productive to the spirit in which Bally Arcade was created.  I know that other systems like the Apple II were programmed like this sometimes, and it would be a wonderful tech demo to program using this low level method, but I still believe strongly that programs on the astrocade could be created as they were originally intended: machine language using low resolution, or, if available (as it was in the arcade systems) programming in machine language using high-resolution.

Since Steve's project, in some way, might allow the high-resolution of the Astrocade to come into being in some manner, I'd like to throw my weight behind it.

Adam

There is an area of "overscan" called the vertical retrace area. This area is where the TY studios used to do such things as sync the scan oascillators (both Vert and Horiz), syncronize the colors, and various other items. This was evident whin you were able to tae the Vert hold control and turn it so that you could see the "blacker-than-black" bar. In the middle was the "Belt and Buckle" which was all of the studio's scratchpad. in B&W sets it was various shades orf gray. The color sets looked much prettier. This area, verticle retrace, is where good programmers do a lot of overhead like do the math and "show" for the moving of the gtraphics. This way, when the signal came out of retrace, it was already in the RAM, ready to be displayed. WOW, my 50+ years in TV repair has brought back many memories.

While there is a long tradition of using the overscan area of many home computers, it's probably best not to use tricks like this one.

16922:
The Astrocade Keyboard is very simply a switching matrix that is also shared with the joyports.
there is actually room in that switching matrix for the addition of more keys or firing buttons.
They are just not hooked up to anything in the Astrocade. The I/O chip uses an 8 by 8
matrix read from ports 10H through 17H. There are 20 switch bits not used in the Astrocade.
12 are available on the joy ports 10H through 13H and 8 on the keypad ports 14h through
17H. As it stands, one could add 20 more keys to the pad or 20 more joy inputs with no
interference, one with the other as these switches are all scaned as a pair of 8 x 8 bits.
I do intend to make use of the extra bits that DNA did not back in the day.
--

From: Michael Matte

To: Ken Lill
Cc: Adam Trionfo; Lance Squire
Subject: Perkins Hi-Res RAM Scheme

Hi Ken. It's been a while since I have communicated with you. I have some hi-res news I believe you will be interested in. As you know, I am fascinated with the hi-res capability of the custom Bally Address/Data chips. Up to now, I have seen 6 hi-res screen RAM interfacing scheme variations. There are two Seawolf II schemes plus the DataMax UV-1R scheme which are posted on the Bally Alley. I created 2 scheme variations, one of which utilizes static screen RAM. The sixth scheme variation is by Perkins Engineering. The other day, I was browsing the Bally Alley, as I sometimes do, enjoying all the hi-res documentation. I looked at your photos of the Perkins hi-res scheme. I was intrigued once again by this scheme. I took time and made some notes related to what I was and wasn't seeing in these photos. I also checked out my emails related to Perkins scheme and its hi-res Basic. The other day, I was again on the Bally Alley, this time browsing the Perkins section. To my surprise, I accidentally stumbled upon the Perkins hi-res RAM interfacing schematic. Wow! Hopefully, the link below will get you to the Perkins hi-res schematic.

https://ballyalley.com/perkins/perkins.html#Perkins_Bally_Astrocade_Hi-Res_Schematics

This schematic is loaded with interfacing details. I believe, because of my experience in hi-res screen RAM interfacing and having discovered this Perkins schematic, I have unlocked a mystery related to the Perkins hi-res modification for the Bally/Astrocade motherboard. I believe I can decipher this schematic and figure out how the Perkins scheme works. I am excited about this discovery and am planning some time later on to spend more time investigating this scheme further. I already wrote down a bunch of comments related to this scheme. Below are a few of the comments I noted just looking at the Perkins schematic recently, that you might find of value. By the way, this may be the only documentation that Perkins drew up relating to this scheme. I say this because this drawing is very detailed and looks nearly complete. The only thing that is probably missing is the actual wiring to the screen RAM. That really would have to be drawn on a separate page but, in this case, is not necessary for anyone experienced with Bally/Astrocade screen DRAM interfacing.


1. Added Chips

All 39 chips are listed on the schematic.

There is no RAM address A0-A5 buffer 74LS244 (or equal) listed.

There is no RAM data in (DI) buffer 74LS244 (or equal) listed.

There is no RAM DI/DO transceiver 74LS245 (or equal) listed.

74LS165 chips are used instead of 74LS166.

DM81LS95 chips are used instead of 74LS253.

A 4K x 8 bit 2732 EPROM is listed.


Question A, Is there a wrapping wire soldered to the EPROM active low chip select (CS)?


Question B, Is this EPROM wired for 4k or 2KB? Check if the A11 pin is grounded or at +5V.


2. Seven Single Piggyback Chips

These 7 chips are labeled showing what motherboard U chip they are sitting on top of.

For example, at the bottom of Perkins schematic, LS175 (number 1) is labeled as being on the motherboard chip U8.


3. Logic Scheme At Very Top Of Perkins Schematic Using LS27, LS20, LS74, LS00

This is an output port outputting Z80 bits D0 and D1 to this port.

It's purpose is not clear at this time. Further investigation is required.


Motherboard ROMs active low chip select (CS) is wired to LS20B input.


Pin 11 of LS00B is wired to ROM U2, pin 20 (CS).

Is this labeled correctly? Should this be labeled as U4?

The Bally Service Manual on the motherboard layout drawing, indicates the EPROM location should be designated as U4.

Further investigation of this decoder is required.


4. LS175 Chip (Number 1, On Top Of U8)

RAS1, RAS2, and RAS3 are wired here to pins 4, 5 and 13 respectively. Pin number 12 is NOT wired to RAS0.

Looks like RAS0 is left pretty much "as is" on the motherboard.

There are some minor rewires to the motherboard indicated on the bottom of Perkins schematic related to RAS0 thru RAS3.


5. Bottom Left-Hand Corner on Perkins Schematic

Looks like there are only 5 breaks in motherboard traces.

Ditto marks mean?


6. Top Right-Hand Corner Of Perkins Schematic

There are 8 four-tier RAM towers.

The towers are located/labeled as 0 thru 7 matching the Bally motherboard layout.

The bottom tier, the standard DRAM chips U24 thru U31, are soldered completely into motherboard and are probably labeled as RAM Bank 0.

The top tier is probably RAM Bank 3.


7. Tower U23

Question C, Does this tower have only four DM81LS95 chips?

Line Side Of Chips (All 4 Chips)

MD0-MD7 are all wired to the custom data chip.

Not Shown! All MD0-MD7 lines are wired directly to the respective RAM data input (DI) pins 2 for all 4 RAM banks.

Looks like the custom data chip MD0-MD7 pins are driving all the RAM DI inputs. There is no buffer chip listed in the 39 chips list for this application. This is outside the norm. That means, for example, that the custom data line MD0, pin 28 is likely driving 4 RAM DI, pin 2 chips and is also wired to pin 17 of all  4 DM81LS95 chips.

Load Side Of Chips (all 4 Chips)

Perkins indicates where the load side wiring is connected to the data out (DO, pin 14) RAM chip pins by labeling the RAM connections at the right side of the four LS95 chips.

For example, at LS95 (number 0), pin 16 is wired to pin 14 of the RAM chip 1 in Bank 0.


8. Tower U20

Question D, Does this tower have 5 chips?

Question E, Is the bottom chip completely soldered into the motherboard?

If the Question E answer is yes, this is probably the standard U20, 74LS174 chip.

If this is so, this 74LS174 chip is likely driving all 32 chips for each of the address lines A0-A5. There is no buffer chip 74LS244 (or equal) listed in the 39 chips listing.

This means, for example, U20, output pin 15 is driving 32 RAM chip A0, pin 5 inputs. Ouch! This is outside the norm. If this is indeed the case for this modification scheme, apparently this bufferless set up still functions correctly.

There must be four 74LS165 chips on this tower. Ken's photos show multiple wrapping wires from tower U20 to tower U23. A total of 32 lines must be wired from the four LS165 chip RAM read inputs to the four LS95 chips. The four LS165 chips are used for the hi-res TV display scan. The RAM TV display read (scan) data is shifted serially along Serial 0 and Serial 1 lines to the custom data chip at its input pins 11 and 12. This scan may also serve to refresh the RAM row addresses.

Serial 0 is wired to pin 9, LS165 (number 0). Serial 1 is wired to pin 9, LS165 (number 2).

These 4 chips are clocked at pin 2 using the active low inverted 7M clock (pin 3 from U32).

The Shift Load line S/L is at pin 1 for all four chips.

A TV display read (scan) occurs when all four RAS lines are active high simultaneously. Four bytes at a time are read. The Shift Load line goes active low shortly after the four RAS lines are all active high simultaneously. The active low S/L line tells the four LS165 chips when to shift serially the four bytes of data into the custom data chip via the Serial 0 and Serial 1 lines.

Why was type 74LS165 chips used instead of the normal 74LS166?

Is this related to the medium-res mode?

Is the medium-res mode an undocumented optional mode for the custom address/data chips or is this mode generated using screen interrupts?

Why was the 74LS165 designation in this tower of chips "blacked out"?

Maybe only the top chip was "blacked out".

Note that MCM Design has accidentally found out that because the hi-res TV display is scanned and fed into the custom data chip Serial 0 and Serial 1 inputs, no screen RAM is actually required to display a simple hi-res graphic test pattern of vertical stripes on the TV. The test pattern can be created simply by "floating" and grounding specific "read" RAM data out lines at the four LS165 chip 32 read inputs. Think of the 32 inputs as four bytes or 16 pixels. Note also that to run this TV display test pattern, the 32 read input lines at the four LS165 chips can NOT be connected to the 32 RAM data output pins. To display a test pattern, a ML program must be executed to disable any screen interrupts, set up normal screen parameters, then "halt" the Z80 CPU. For more information on this unusual hi-res test, contact MCM Design.

Question E, When Ken had his Perkins hi-res motherboard running, did he actually see the low-res menu running in the upper left quadrant on the TV screen?

In one of Ken's Perkins hi-res motherboard photo, you can see 2 blue wrapping wires from the custom data chip, pins 11 and 12, Serial 0 and Serial 1 lines heading toward the tower 20.


Miscellaneous Comments

Question F, Does KEN have the power supply transformer to power his Perkins board?

MCM Design's BalcheckHR has a hi-res screen RAM test and also SetScreenHR to help troubleshoot a modified for hi-res Bally/Astrocade motherboard.

MCM Design plans to investigate Perkins hi-res scheme further sometime after the hi-res static screen RAM multi-pager demo and the hi-res demos on a DVD projects are completed.

Ken, at your convenience, could you take a look at your Perkins hi-res board and answer the above Questions A thru F? This would help me understand how Perkins hi-res scheme works. Who knows, after I complete my investigation, we might be able to troubleshoot your Perkins motherboard and get it up and running. Wouldn't that be cool.

Bye.
MCM

For stupidly redundant purposes, The names of the systems and companies went like this,

Bally/Home Library Computer -> Bally
Bally/Professional Arcade -> Bally
Bally/Computer System -> Bally for a short time.

(internally Bally called it the home arcade or just arcade)

Astrovision acquires the units...

Bally/Computer System -> Astrovision

As the time to use the Bally name was running out,
Astro/Professional Arcade was proposed but never released as Astrovision found they had a name clash with co selling video equipment.

Changed its name to Astrocade. Marketing proposes

Astrocade inc./Professional Arcade

Seen on box art. Finally released as:

ASTROCADE
the professional arcade

But many boxes from Astrocade contain Bally labels as they had so much stock.

So I usually call it the Bally/Astrocade, listing the two companies marketing it. Bally & Astrovision/Astrocade

Lance

From: Michael Matte

To: Ken Lill
Cc: Adam Trionfo, Lance Squire
Subject: Perkins Investigation Report 1


PERKINS HI-RES MODIFICATION SCHEME, REPORT 1

BY MCM DESIGN

I have spent time investigating the logic scheme, at the very top of Perkins interfacing schematic, using the LS27, LS20, LS74 and LS00 chips. Here are my findings in my first report. First, thanks to Ken Lill's email statement to me relating to the custom 2KB ROM chips internal wiring of address lines A11 and A12, the 4 ROM chips are addressed as indicated below.

Board  MFGR
Label   Label

   U4      HVSA  0000-07FFH
   U2      HVSC  0800-0FFFH
   U3      HVSB  1000-17FFH
   U1      HVSD  1800-1FFFH

Operating System     0000-0E18H

3 Games, Calculator 0E19-1FFFH

A 24 pin wire wrap socket, with its posts trimmed, is soldered into the motherboard at the ROM chip location U4.

The 4K x 8 bit 2732 EPROM is installed into the WW socket.

Ken's photos do NOT reveal how the right side of the EPROM is wired, in particular, the EPROM's pin 21 (A11) and pin 18 (active low E?).

The Perkins photocopied schematic is "clipped off" on the very top of the schematic.

The LS27 chip contains triple 3-input NOR gates.

Because of the photo clip, 5 chip pins are subject to speculation regarding where they are wired to. One of Ken's photo may reveal one connection. Here's my speculation.

1. LS27A, pin 13 (on top of U13) is wired to the Z80 address A0 line, possibly at U9, pin 2.

2. LS20A, pin 13 (on top of U14) is wired to the Z80 address A3 line, possibly at U4, pin 5.

3. The LS74 A and B clear (clr) pins 13 and 1 (on top of U21) may be wired to the 1.0 MFD "reset" capacitor C13 (positive end). This cap is wired to the system reset button. This capacitor is shown on the Bally PA-1 Service Manual motherboard layout and schematic. Another option is that the 2 clear pins are wired to +5V.

4. LS00A, pin 9 (on top of U22) is connected to LS20B, pin 6 by wiring this pin 9 to its neighboring pin 13 on LS00B.

5. LS00A, pin 8 is wired to the U4 EPROM chip select, pin 20.

The LS27, LS20 and LS74 logic scheme is a custom output port 08H. The output D0 bit to LS74A, pin 12 is used to decode EPROM U4 and ROM U2 for hi-res and low-res operation. LS00B is used to decode and select ROM U2 in the low-res mode. This part of my speculation is not clear to me at this time, possibly because of the missing wiring in the photocopy "clip off". This is why I want to decode the EPROM power up routine. It is not clear to me at this time, how the EPROM can distinguish between a low-res or a hi-res mode request to output port 08H. A part of the EPROM must include the low-res operating system. How much of the 4KB EPROM is used for the hi-res and med-res modes is unknown at this time. An examination of the EPROM's hex coding would help answer that question.

The custom output port 08H, bit D1 is related to the hi-res video scan, to possibly enable the inverted 7M clock scan for hi-res and possibly inhibit this clock for low-res, so the low-res video scan can be fed into the custom data MD0-MD7 lines. This scheme will be investigated later.

I loaded Ken's EPROM bin file into a hex editor and printed out a hex dump of the entire 4KB. I have examined some of the coding and have deemed this bin file as bad (inaccurate). I emailed my reasons to Adam Trionfo. I can say the following with some certainty.

1. Some of the coding at the EPROM location 0000H+ is an inaccurate copy of the low-res ROM operating system.

2. There is NO low-res output request to port 08H at address 0003H.

3. At address 0005H, there is a Z80 jump C3 61 0C code to the power up routine (just like the low-res ROM). I will not attempt to decode the power up routine now because I have deemed the coding there as untrustworthy.

In conclusion, my Perkins hi-res modification scheme investigation is "on hold". I have gone as far as I can with my investigation of this 8 gate output port/ROM decoder scheme at the top of Perkins interfacing scheme. In order to further investigate this scheme to understand how the U4 EPROM functions, I need:

1. Clear photos or "word-of-mouth" info detailing the missing 5 pin wiring on the top of Perkins schematic described in my above speculation and also the wiring on the right side of the EPROM as mentioned above.

2. An accurate hex dump of the EPROM, so I can at least decode the power up routine.

I plan to, some time later, continue my investigation as to why Perkins chose to use 74LS165 chips instead of the normal 74LS166 chips. I plan to redraw the 74LS165 scheme and also the RAS0-RAS3 timing scheme shown at the bottom of Perkin's schematic, so the wiring is easier for me to read (interpret). Perhaps this future part of the investigation may provide clues as to how the EPROM is utilized. Wish me luck.

End Of Report 1

MCM Design
March 2020

I added an article to BallyAlley.com called "Hacking 'Astro Battle' ('Space Invaders') on the Bally Arcade/Astrocade" by Adam Trionfo.

This article, which I compiled today, is an edited and expanded collection of postings originally made to the Bally Alley discussion group in August of 2011 that give an overview of how to modify the "Astro Battle" game cartridge, which is Astrocade, Inc.'s 1979 version of "Space Invaders." Included is the binary ROM image for a hack to get rid of the bunkers in the game as well as explanations on how to hack the ROM or use an available Z80 disassembly of the game to make more modifications, such as adding up to 255 lives.

Other members of the Bally Alley discussion group, especially Lance Squire, added plenty of their own work to the threads that eventually sprang forth from the original topic of discussion.

You can read the article here and download the binary for a few of the hacks, here:

https://ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/Hacking_Astro_Battle/Hacking_Astro_Battle.html

This article may seem a bit piece-meal, but I did my best to include the important information from the threads that took place on the Bally Alley discussion group. I have wanted to post this as an article for nine years but I wanted to make it "perfect" first.  I realize I don't have time for that to happen, so sometimes the tense in this article might seem a little "off." Also, if any information seems missing from this compiled article, then read the individual postings at Groups.io.

I was prompted to write this article when Michael Matte asked me some questions on how to use a Windows hex editor.  I thought I'd make a video using a hex editor to hack "Astro Battle" to get extra lives.  This provoked me to re-visit these original hacking posts and I was able to pull an article together with the various threads that materialized back in August 2011.

I have hopes that this article will inspire non-hackers to hack an Astocade game for the first time.  I promise, it's not as hard as you think

Have fun!

Adam

Here are the latest hi-res updates from Michael Matte concerning the one-of-a-kind hi-res Astrocade that was made by Perkins Engineering in the early 1980s.

----------------------------------------

From: Michael Matte
Sent: Tuesday, March 3, 2020 7:55 PM
To: Adam Trionfo
Cc: Lance Squire
Subject: Perkins Hi-Res Scheme
 
Last evening I just had to take one last look at the Perkins hi-res modification scheme, before I put aside my investigation of this scheme for perhaps a month or more. I have come up with 2 theories related to Perkins scheme.

Theory 1

The medium-res map of 160 x 204 pixels will be displayed on a TV/monitor by outputting 0000 0011 (03H) to port 08H. The Perkins scheme has the option to inhibit the inverted 7M clock that is used for the hi-res video display scan. This option maps out the medium-res video display. This is a very cleverly designed option.

The 74LS165 chip has a clock inhibit input. My 74LS data book indicated that the clock input is inhibited when the CI input is high. The Perkins inhibit logic scheme utilizes the LS74 (a custom 08H output port), LS00D and LS00C gates. The motherboard PX clock is input to the LS00D, pin 2. The PX clock frequency is twice as slow as the inverted 7M clock. Normally, the hi-res video scan reads 4 bytes (16 pixels) at a time. As I see it, when 03H is output to port 08H, every other 7M clock tick high will be inhibited (shut off). The hi-res video scan will continue reading 4 bytes at a time, but only 2 bytes (8 pixels) of the 16 pixel data will be shifted out, from the four 74LS165 chip inputs, into the custom data chip Serial 0 and Serial 1 input lines, mapping out only 160 pixels on the screen horizontal line instead of 320 pixels. All 204 hi-res horizontal lines will be scanned and mapped out onto the TV screen. The med-res mode utilizes only RAM banks 0 and 1.

Theory 2

74LS166 chips can be substituted for 74LS165 chips. However, the pin layouts are not compatible.

Action To Take

I plan much later to test these 2 theories on my hi-res static screen RAM prototype board, to see if the theories are correct.

I also may be able to utilize a portion of the Perkins scheme to simplify the hi-res video scan scheme on my hi-res static screen RAM board.

I will email you the results of these experiments when they are run.

Bye.

MCM

----------------------------------------

It neat to see this project evolve in small steps.  I really think it's great that despite the obstacles, Michael has been able to persevere and keep his heart and mind interested in his hi-res Astrocade project off and on since 1986 or so; that's kind of mind boggling to me.

Adam

This article, which I compiled today, is an edited and expanded collection of postings originally made to the Bally Alley discussion group in August of 2011 that give an overview of how to modify the "Astro Battle" game cartridge, which is Astrocade, Inc.'s 1979 version of "Space Invaders." Included is the binary ROM image for a hack to get rid of the bunkers in the game as well as explanations on how to hack the ROM or use an available Z80 disassembly of the game to make more modifications, such as adding up to 255 lives.

Other members of the Bally Alley discussion group, especially Lance Squire, added plenty of their own work to the threads that eventually sprang forth from the original topic of discussion.

You can read the article here and download the binary for a few of the hacks, here:

https://ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/Hacking_Astro_Battle/Hacking_Astro_Battle.html
This article may seem a bit piece-meal, but I did my best to include the important information from the threads that took place on the Bally Alley discussion group. I have wanted to post this as an article for nine years but I wanted to make it "perfect" first.  I realize I don't have time for that to happen, so sometimes the tense in this article might seem a little "off." Also, if any information seems missing from this compiled article, then read the individual postings at Groups.io.

I was prompted to write this article when Michael Matte asked me some questions on how to use a Windows hex editor.  I thought I'd make a video using a hex editor to hack "Astro Battle" to get extra lives.  This provoked me to re-visit these original hacking posts and I was able to pull an article together with the various threads that materialized back in August 2011.

I have hopes that this article will inspire non-hackers to hack an Astocade game for the first time.  I promise, it's not as hard as you think

Have fun!

Adam

"Astro Battle" was probably rushed-out the door, which is why the game ends.  One example that might prove this idea to be true is that "Astro Battle" only uses about 3K of the 4K cartridge ROM.  This means that there was plenty of other space on the cartridge to make additions or changes to the game without much trouble.  Many players probably never made it to level 6 or 7 of the game to see it stop, I don't think that I ever made it that far into the game.

Or maybe it's as simple as the programmer thinking that getting to the level where the Invaders land no matter how good the player is at the game just proves true that you can't forever stop an invasion fleet.  With enough ships, the Invaders always win.  This ain't so much an Astro Battle and an Invasion Slaughter.

Adam

Adam,

A small aside...

Action Graphics contracted me to do cartridges after I did "Treasure Cove" and "ICBM Attack" on my own.

I had written my cartridges in Z80 assembler on a development system we (Spectre) created.

Action Graphics provided me with a DataMax UV-1 game development system running Terse Forth.

They had wanted me to work on "Cosmic Raiders" (i.e. Defenders), but I had a horrible time adapting to using Terse Forth as a development language.

Hey, Kevin, that is great news that you were finally able to get your expanded RAM working with your astrocade.  Removing the breakout-panel from the back of the Astocade can be a chore, but once it is has been done, then you never have to do it again.  You will also notice that removing anything hooked up to the 50-pin connection in the back of the astrocade isn't a trivial task either; the hardware tends to hold onto the bus tightly.

You asked for some recommendation on expansion RAM software to use.  I can't remember which programs will load using the Lil' White RAM; I think many of the 2000-Baud programs require a Blue Ram Expansion for its I/O interface.  Still... how about some of these programs:

1) "Viper Test Pattern" By Alternative Engineering - This one is just a quick type-in that will allow you to use some of the extra features of ViperSoft BASIC:

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/ram_expansion_required/alternative_engineering/alternative_engineering.html

2) Any video art by Stan Kendall is worth trying:

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/ram_expansion_required/Stanley_Kendall/Stanley_Kendall.html

3) Mike Peace probably took advantage of expansion RAM more than anyone else for use with games:

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/ram_expansion_required/WaveMakers(EB)/WaveMakers(EB).html

You probably have already visited this area of ballyalley.com, but this is where all of the expansion RAM programs are available:

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/ram_expansion_required/ram_expansion_required.html

You have already tried out expansion RAM programs using the UltiMulti cart.  That is probably the easiest and best way to use the Lil' White RAM; after all, it was created expressly for that purpose.

Keep us up-to-date with your experience with your new RAM expansion.

Adam

Here is lite pen information from Mike White's "The Bally Astrocade Hardware Guide: Plans, Prototypes and Production:"

https://ballyalley.com/faqs/bally_astrocade_hardware_guide_faq.txt

LITE PEN [proto] This was asked for on page 19 of the second Arcadian and mentioned on page 37 (along with its apparent problems). Three schemes were promised in print!  The Blue RAM ad on page 68 was the first, while the write-up on the "ZGRASS 32" on page 82 of Cursor (74) was the second.  The third was on page 85 of the fourth Arcadian, where the "CREATIVE CRAYON WITH LITE PEN 4005P" turned up.
     None of these ever materialized!  Greg Anderson demonstrated one that he built (75), later listing one in the Sourcebooks as "THE COMPUTER EYE" by H.A.R.D.; but no ad appeared in any of the newsletters!
     Two "bugs members" were said to have working prototypes on the second page of the 3/84 AstroBugs; the page later appeared as a copy in the Arcadian (76). The only other unit I know of was made by Leroy Flamm, who wrote his own software to make it work (77)!

A light pen is talked about in this article:

https://ballyalley.com/articles_and_news/BUG%20Gets%20a%20Look%20at%20ZGrass-32/BUG%20Gets%20a%20Look%20at%20ZGrass-32.html

If you search around BallyAlley.com, then you'll find some (very) rough plans for some lite pens, but there isn't really any software for them.

The expanded RAM version of "Outpost 19" is pretty good and it works from the UltiMulti cart.  This updated "AstroBASIC" game takes advantage of many of the new features of Blue RAM BASIC.  You'll see such extra features used as:

1) Additional graphics made possible by the extra RAM.
2) Music, which is possible through the PLAY command.
3) Four colors, 4 bits per pixel, just like a cartridge.

In an upcoming episode of the Astrocast, Chris and I will be reviewing "Outpost 19" for "AstroBASIC."  We played quite a bit of the original version of this game in preparation for Astrocast #13, but we didn't have time to record a review.
